summary: Discusses how ICMP can be used to attack TCP connections, and describes widely implemented changes to TCP's handling of ICMP error messages that reduce these attacks. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Tricking a computer with fake error notes so it hangs up a call. It also describes how computers learned to doubt those notes.

subtitle: How forged ICMP error messages can reset, slow or cripple a TCP connection, and the checks that stop them.

tldr.problem: TCP is told to act on ICMP error messages without checking them, so an off-path attacker who can guess a connection's four-tuple can forge errors that reset the connection, slow it down or shrink its packets.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC documents widely implemented checks: validate the TCP sequence number inside the ICMP payload, treat ICMP hard errors as soft errors on established connections, ignore Source Quench, and delay acting on Packet Too Big messages until a segment times out.
tldr.outcome: These counter-measures are not part of standard TCP behavior and this RFC does not change the TCP standard. It documents existing practice, at the cost of sometimes reacting more slowly to genuine errors.

today: RFC 5927 is an Informational RFC and its metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It documents existing nonstandard TCP behavior rather than defining a standard.

sections.title: Why ICMP Can Be Used Against TCP
sections.content:
ICMP is mainly used to report network errors. The existing specifications do not recommend any validation checks on received ICMP error messages, which allows three kinds of attack on TCP: blind connection-reset, blind throughput-reduction and blind performance-degrading attacks. All can be done by an off-path attacker who cannot see the connection's packets.

A 2005 disclosure process coordinated by the UK's NISCC (now CPNI) found a large number of implementations vulnerable to all or some of these attacks, from desktop stacks to core routers.

The counter-measures here are not part of standard TCP behavior. The TCPM working group chose to document this widespread nonstandard behavior without changing the TCP standard.
sections.eli5: Error notes are meant to help, but nobody checked who wrote them. That lets a stranger send fake notes that make a conversation stop or slow down.

sections.title: How TCP Treats ICMP Errors
sections.content:
ICMP error messages carry part of the packet that triggered them, so the receiver can match the error to a connection. RFC 1122 says TCP MUST act on an ICMP error passed up from IP, and neither it nor the original TCP specification recommends any validation. As long as the payload identifies an existing connection, TCP acts on it.

An attacker therefore needs the four-tuple: source address, source port, destination address and destination port. Usually that is unknown, but for some connections, such as those between two BGP routers, it can be guessed. If only the client port is unknown, at most 65536 packets are needed in principle. Many systems pick outgoing ports from a subset of the port space, which makes it easier still.
sections.eli5: If a stranger knows which two people are talking and which phone lines they use, they can send a fake message that looks like it belongs to that call.

sections.title: General Counter-Measures
sections.content:
Checks are limited by how much of the original packet the ICMP message contains. For ICMPv4 hosts, you can only expect the IP header plus the first 64 bits of the payload, which for TCP means the two ports and the 32-bit sequence number. Authentication such as the TCP MD5 option or IPsec cannot be recomputed from that fragment, and requiring authenticated ICMP from every router is not feasible.

  • Sequence number checking: accept an ICMP error only if the sequence number is in SND.UNA =< SEG.SEQ < SND.NXT, meaning data sent but not yet acknowledged. The chance of a spoofed message passing drops to Flight_Size/2^32, and with no data in flight it drops to zero.
  • Port randomization: a wider, randomized range of ephemeral ports makes the four-tuple harder to guess.
  • Payload filtering: firewalls and NATs can filter on the source address of the IP header inside the ICMP payload, since that address must be spoofed for these attacks to work.

The sequence check does not help against on-path attackers, and it may discard legitimate errors because ICMP has no timeliness requirements.
sections.eli5: The first defense is to ask whether the note talks about a message you really sent and have not heard back about. A note about something you never sent is thrown away.

sections.title: Reset and Throughput Attacks
sections.content:
In the connection-reset attack, the attacker sends an ICMP hard error, and TCP aborts the connection. RFC 1122 lists type 3 codes 2, 3 and 4 as hard errors, and some stacks even apply one error to every connection between the same peers. This works even if TCP is protected by MD5, TCP-AO or network-layer authentication. The counter-measure used by most popular implementations is to treat hard errors on synchronized connections as soft errors, so TCP keeps retransmitting until the connection times out. This may delay a response to a genuine error, and applications can still abort on their own.

In the throughput-reduction attack, forged ICMPv4 Source Quench messages (type 4, code 0) make TCP slow down, and a sustained attack can reduce throughput to about SMSS bytes per RTT. RFC 1812 says routers SHOULD NOT send Source Quench for congestion, and TCP has its own congestion control, so many implementations ignore Source Quench for TCP. That violates the RFC 1122 requirement to react.
sections.eli5: A fake 'stop, the road is closed' note can make a driver turn back, or a fake 'slow down' note can make a driver crawl. The fix is to keep driving unless the problem is real.

sections.title: The Path MTU Attack and Its Fix
sections.content:
Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD) lets a sender learn the largest packet that fits along a path, using ICMPv4 'fragmentation needed and DF set' (type 3, code 4) or ICMPv6 'Packet Too Big' (type 2, code 0). An attacker can forge one advertising a tiny Next-Hop MTU. For IPv4 it can be as small as 68 octets, so packets shrink, header overhead grows and the sender needs a higher packet rate for the same throughput.

The RFC says Packetization Layer PMTUD, which does not depend on ICMP, removes the vulnerability but can slow convergence. It also describes a change in OpenBSD and NetBSD (since 2005) that splits PMTUD into two stages, using the variables maxsizesent and maxsizeacked:

  • If the claimed MTU is larger than maxsizesent, the message is silently discarded.
  • If it is at least maxsizeacked, TCP is in the initial discovery stage and honors it immediately.
  • If it is smaller than maxsizeacked, the error is only recorded and honored after the segment times out MAXSEGRTO times. If the sequence number is acknowledged first, the pending error is cleared.

Both OpenBSD and NetBSD set MAXSEGRTO to 1. The RFC also works through five scenarios and gives pseudo-code.
sections.eli5: Telling a truck driver 'only tiny parcels fit' makes them make lots of tiny trips. So the driver waits and checks whether big parcels were actually getting through before believing it.

sections.title: Costs and Scope
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section sums up the trade-offs. Treating hard errors as soft errors trades some responsiveness for robustness. Ignoring Source Quench matches research showing it is an ineffective and unfair antidote for congestion. The delayed Packet Too Big handling parallels PLPMTUD, and in some scenarios TCP may respond more slowly to valid messages.

The RFC does not address the functionality problems of PMTUD described in RFC 2923, and points to RFC 4821 for a mechanism that does.
sections.eli5: Being careful means you sometimes react a little late to a real warning. The RFC says that is a fair price for not being tricked.
